content.overview: BNS s. 24 — Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated. BNS restatement of IPC 86. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 86. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 24 is the rule on “Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated”. The section provides that in cases where an act done is not an offence unless done with a particular knowledge or intent, a person who does the act in a state of intoxication shall be liable to be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge as he would have had if he had not been intoxicated, unless the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 24 exists so that “Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
24. In cases where an act done is not an offence unless done with a particular knowledge or intent, a person who does the act in a state of intoxication shall be liable to be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge as he would have had if he had not been intoxicated, unless the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will

Essential ingredients
1. In cases where an act done is not an offence unless done with a particular knowledge or intent, a person who does the act in a state of intoxication shall be liable to be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge as he would have had if he had not been intoxicated, unless the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will

learningObjectives: Analyze the legal presumption regarding knowledge in voluntary intoxication cases under BNS s. 24.
Distinguish between legal presumption of 'knowledge' and factual inquiry into 'particular intent'.
Understand when extreme intoxication may negate specific intent while leaving liability based on knowledge intact.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 24 provides that in cases where an act done is not an offence unless done with a particular knowledge or intent, a person who does the act in a state of intoxication shall be liable to be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge as he would have had if he had not been intoxicated, unless the thing which intoxicated him was administered to him without his knowledge or against his will.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Under voluntary intoxication, the law imputes constructive knowledge to the actor. A voluntarily intoxicated person is judged as if he possessed the knowledge of a sober person. However, specific criminal intent (mens rea in the strict sense) cannot be automatically imputed and remains a matter of factual determination based on evidence.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 24 (corresponding to IPC s. 86).
Scope: Applies to offences requiring 'a particular knowledge or intent' (e.g. murder, housebreaking by night).
Statutory fiction / presumption: The person is liable to be dealt with 'as if he had the same knowledge' as a sober person.
Omission of 'intent': The statute deliberately imputes knowledge, not intent. Intent must be proved as a fact or inferred from surrounding acts.
Proviso / Exception: Involuntary intoxication is excluded and remains governed by s. 23.
essentialIngredients: The offence charged requires proof of a particular knowledge or specific intent.
The accused committed the act while in a state of voluntary intoxication.
By statutory fiction, the accused is presumed to possess the same knowledge as a sober person in that situation.
Specific intent is not presumed by law; it must be gathered from all proved facts, including the degree of intoxication.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 24 prevents a voluntary drinker from pleading drunkenness as a general licence for crime. The law creates an artificial rule of liability: the voluntarily intoxicated person cannot say 'I was drunk, so I did not know striking someone with a heavy rod was dangerous'. The law treats him as having the knowledge of a sober person. However, where an offence requires a particular or specific intention (such as premeditated murder under BNS s. 101/103), the court must determine whether the accused was so thoroughly incapacitated that he was incapable of forming any intent at all. If the evidence shows he was drunk but still capable of forming intent, or if his actions were coordinated, intent is proved and the offence is complete.
examples: Teaching example (Knowledge imputed): A man gets voluntarily drunk at a festival, picks up a loaded shotgun, and fires into a crowd. He claims he did not realize shooting into a crowd would kill anyone. Under s. 24, he is dealt with as having the knowledge of a sober person that firing into a crowd is imminently dangerous.

Teaching example (Intent vs Knowledge): An intoxicated person enters another's house at night and collapses on the rug asleep. He is prosecuted for housebreaking with intent to commit theft. While knowledge of entry is presumed, the specific intent to steal cannot be presumed and may fail on the facts if no theft was planned or attempted.
distinctions: Knowledge vs Intent under s. 24: The statute imputes constructive knowledge, but does not impute constructive intent.
Section 23 vs Section 24: Section 23 governs involuntary intoxication and can excuse the act completely; Section 24 governs voluntary intoxication and restricts defences.
Drunkenness producing disease of mind (delirium tremens): If long-term drinking creates a settled disease of the mind, it is evaluated under s. 22, not s. 24.
problemApplication: Issue: What is the criminal liability of an accused who, while heavily intoxicated, stabbed an acquaintance during a tavern dispute?
Rule: BNS s. 24 imputes knowledge that stabbing causes bodily injury likely to cause death; specific intent to cause death is assessed from the degree of drunkenness, weapon used, and force applied.

Application: If the accused was able to draw the knife, aim for a vital organ, and flee afterwards, his intoxication was not so extreme as to negate intent. If he was in a state of helpless delirium, knowledge is imputed but specific intent may be negatived, leading to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
Conclusion: Voluntary drunkenness does not confer immunity; liability is fixed on imputed knowledge and factual intent.

keyTakeaways: Voluntary intoxication never excuses an offence as of right.
The law presumes the accused had the knowledge of a sober person.
Specific intent is not presumed, but inferred from the accused's acts and surrounding facts.
